questions.question: JavaScript is single-threaded. How can it handle a timer, a click and a network response at the same time without freezing?
questions.answer:
It does not run them at the same time on the JavaScript thread. The engine runs one call stack, and slow work such as timers, network I/O and input is handled by the host environment (browser or Node). When that work completes, its callback is placed in a queue. The event loop takes one task from the queue, runs it to completion, drains the microtask queue, and then repeats.

The single thread is why a long synchronous loop blocks clicks and rendering: the loop cannot pick up the next task until the stack is empty. Concurrency comes from the host's ability to wait on many operations and queue their callbacks, not from running JavaScript in parallel. True parallelism needs a Web Worker or a Node worker thread, which have their own stacks and event loops.
key_points: One call stack, one task at a time
Host handles timers, I/O and input
Callbacks wait in task/microtask queues
Long sync work blocks everything

questions.question: What is the difference between the task queue and the microtask queue, and why does the distinction matter?
questions.answer:
The task queue (macrotask queue) holds timers, I/O completions and user events. The event loop runs exactly one task per turn. The microtask queue holds Promise reactions, queueMicrotask callbacks and MutationObserver callbacks, and it is drained completely after every task and after every callback during that drain — including microtasks added while draining.

The distinction matters because microtasks always run before the next task, before rendering, and before any timer. That is why a Promise chain resolves before a setTimeout(..., 0), and why an unbounded recursive microtask can starve timers and paint forever. The loop never moves on until the microtask queue is empty.
key_points: One macrotask per turn, all microtasks after it
Microtasks include newly queued microtasks
Microtasks run before rendering and timers
Microtask starvation can freeze the page

questions.answer:
The order is A, F, D, B, C, E.

A and F are synchronous, so they run first. The script ends, and the microtask queue contains the first then callback, which prints D and schedules a new timer E. The queue is now empty, so the loop takes the first timer: it prints B and queues a microtask C. After that task, microtasks drain and C prints. Finally the timer queued from D runs and prints E.

The trap is assuming all timers run before microtasks, or that C waits for another turn. C is queued during a task, so it runs before the next task (E). This pattern — a microtask scheduled inside a task — is exactly why promise callbacks feel immediate compared with timers.
key_points: Sync first: A, F
Microtasks before timers: D
Microtask queued inside a task runs before the next task: C before E
Timers keep FIFO order: B before E

questions.answer:
It prints then 1, then 2, inner micro, timer.

Both then callbacks are queued before the script ends. The queue is [then 1, then 2]. Running then 1 queues inner micro at the back and schedules a timer; the queue is now [then 2, inner micro]. Running then 2 leaves [inner micro], which still drains before the event loop moves to the timer. Only when the microtask queue is empty does the timer task run.

The timer is a macrotask, so it cannot jump ahead of any microtask, even one created after it. Replacing queueMicrotask with setTimeout would put 'inner micro' behind 'timer' and change the order.
key_points: New microtasks go to the back but still drain this turn
then 2 was already queued, so it runs before inner micro
Timers wait until the microtask queue is empty
queueMicrotask vs setTimeout changes the order

questions.question: How does a Web Worker keep the UI responsive, and what can and cannot cross the worker boundary?
questions.answer:
A Web Worker runs on a separate thread with its own call stack and event loop, so CPU-heavy work there does not block the main thread's tasks or rendering. You create it with new Worker(url) (or a Blob URL), send data with worker.postMessage(value), and receive results through worker.onmessage or addEventListener('message').

Data crosses by structured clone: plain objects, arrays, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer and typed arrays are copied. Functions, DOM nodes, class instances with methods and the window object cannot be sent. Transferable objects such as ArrayBuffer can be moved instead of copied by passing them in the transfer list, which is fast but detaches them on the sending side. The worker cannot touch the DOM, so it returns data and the main thread renders it. Terminate with worker.terminate() to free the thread.
key_points: Separate thread and event loop — main thread stays free
postMessage + message event is the only channel
Structured clone copies data; no DOM or functions
Transferables move buffers without copying

questions.question: In Node.js, what is the difference between process.nextTick, Promise microtasks and setImmediate?
questions.answer:
process.nextTick callbacks go into the nextTick queue, which Node drains before the Promise microtask queue and between every phase of the event loop. Promise reactions (and queueMicrotask) go into the V8 microtask queue, drained right after the nextTick queue. setImmediate schedules a callback for the check phase, which runs after the poll phase — so it is a macrotask, not a microtask.

Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout(..., 0): the loop is in poll, then moves to check, while timers are only revisited on the next iteration. At the top level, setTimeout vs setImmediate is nondeterministic and should not be asserted. In browsers there is no setImmediate or process.nextTick; queueMicrotask is the portable microtask API.
key_points: nextTick queue drains before Promise microtasks
Both drain between event-loop phases
setImmediate runs in the check phase, after poll
Inside I/O: setImmediate before setTimeout; top level is nondeterministic
